sections.h2: Does New Jersey have a homestead exemption?
sections.html:
People searching for a New Jersey homestead exemption usually end up at the state's property tax relief programs. The Division of Taxation runs three of them for homeowners: Senior Freeze (Property Tax Reimbursement), ANCHOR and Stay NJ. All three are filed on one combined application, the PAS-1. Municipalities add their own deductions on top.

These programs pay benefits to qualifying owners. They are tied to a principal residence and to income, and eligibility rules, income limits and benefit amounts depend on appropriation in the State Budget, so they can shift from year to year. Check the Division's relief page for the current filing season, and keep your most recent benefit statement and property tax bill handy when you apply.

sections.h2: Which relief program fits which homeowner
sections.html:
The three programs overlap, and the Division decides which benefits an applicant gets. Here is how they compare for the 2025 application year.

Property tax relief programs, 2025 application year
ProgramWho qualifiesIncome limit
ANCHORHomeowners who owned and occupied the home on October 1, 2025, and renters$250,000 for homeowners, $150,000 for renters
Senior FreezeAge 65 or older, or receiving Social Security or Railroad Retirement disability, and owned and lived in the home since December 31, 2022 or earlier$172,475 for 2025
Stay NJHomeowners 65 or older who owned and lived in the home all 12 months of 2025$200,000 or less

A homeowner under 65 who does not receive Social Security disability can qualify only for ANCHOR. A homeowner who is 65 or older may qualify for all three.

The maximum depends on income. For the 2027 payments covering the 2025 tax year, it is $6,500 at income up to $100,000, $5,000 above that through $150,000, and $4,000 above that through $200,000. Over $200,000 the benefit is zero.

Payments arrive in installments, and the 2025 benefit is paid in February and May of 2027. Each applicant gets a benefit statement listing the Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ amounts.

One cap applies to all three programs: total relief cannot exceed the property taxes paid on the principal residence for the qualifying year. Relief payments are not taxable income for New Jersey state taxes.

The home must be your principal residence, meaning the place you live most of the time and where you vote or get mail. For owners it is the property on the deed or tax records. A vacation home, a second home or a rental property does not qualify.

  • Senior Freeze: not available on property with more than four units, or with four units or fewer that contains more than one commercial unit, and not available if you make P.I.L.O.T. payments instead of property tax.
  • Stay NJ: mobile homeowners and renters are excluded, a co-owned home is calculated on your ownership percentage, and a duplex is calculated on the share of the property you occupy.
  • Trusts and life estates: a trust beneficiary, or someone with a life estate or a 99-year lease, can qualify and must send the trust, deed or lease document.

Keep the deed or tax record that names you as owner, since that is what proves the home is your principal residence if a question comes up.

Condominium owners and resident co-op shareholders who pay property tax on their unit count as homeowners.

Municipalities handle several deductions and exemptions directly: a $250 deduction for senior citizens and disabled persons, a $250 deduction for military service, and a 100 percent exemption for service-connected disability.

The senior and disabled deduction has its own tests. The owner must be 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, or an unmarried surviving spouse age 55 or older of such a person. The owner must have lived in New Jersey for a year as of October 1 before the deduction year, owned and lived in the dwelling on that date, and kept income to $10,000 or less with certain exclusions such as Social Security. Form PTD is filed with the municipal assessor or collector, followed by a yearly income statement.

For the military-service programs and the exact forms, call the local tax assessor. These deductions come through the town, not the state application.

sections.h2: What happens to relief benefits if you sell or move
sections.html:
A homeowner who moved during the year is still eligible for ANCHOR, but the benefit follows the qualifying property owned and occupied on October 1. A divorced or separated applicant follows the same test: whoever owned and occupied the home on October 1 may apply.

The closing side works like this. When a benefit check is processed after a move has been properly shown on the application, the money goes to the seller. If the move is not shown, the seller needs to take credit for the benefit at closing, and if the seller, an attorney or the closing agent misses it, the credit lands on the new owners' taxes. That guidance was written for the Homestead Benefit, the earlier program, so ask the title company how current benefits are being handled for your closing.

Senior Freeze recipients who buy another New Jersey home must re-establish eligibility for the new property. A seller who received a reimbursement the year before moving waits two years for a new base year instead of the standard three, then files Form PTR-1-C.

sections.h2: Other tax breaks when selling a New Jersey home
sections.html:
Sales tax is not due on a home sale, and the seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee. Every seller furnishes a GIT/REP form to record the deed, and New Jersey residents use GIT/REP-3 to avoid an estimated income tax payment at closing.

A seller who qualifies for the federal principal residence exclusion can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, after owning and living in the home two of the last five years. Nonresident sellers face an estimated payment of 2 percent of the sale price or 8.97 percent of net gain unless an exemption applies.

The transfer fee is figured per $500 of consideration, with rates that step up as the price rises and an extra Graduated Percent Fee on residential sales above $1,000,000. Ask your closing attorney for the exact fee and for which GIT/REP form you should sign, and gather your benefit statements so the title company can sort out any credit due at closing.

faqs.q: Is there a homestead exemption that lowers my assessed value?
faqs.a: No single program works that way. New Jersey offers ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ as payments through the state, plus local deductions such as the $250 senior and disabled deduction handled by your municipality.

faqs.q: Who qualifies for ANCHOR as a homeowner?
faqs.a: A New Jersey resident who owned and lived in the home on October 1, 2025, with gross income up to $250,000. Renters qualify with income up to $150,000. The home must be the principal residence.

faqs.q: Can I get Stay NJ if I am under 65?
faqs.a: No. You or your spouse must have been 65 or older in 2025, and receiving Social Security disability does not change that. Mobile homeowners and renters are also excluded.

faqs.q: What if I sold my house after filing the relief application?
faqs.a: The benefit follows the home you owned and occupied on October 1. Show the move on the application, or take credit at closing, so the benefit does not pass to the new owners.

faqs.q: Do relief payments count as taxable income in New Jersey?
faqs.a: No. Relief payments are not taxable income for New Jersey state taxes. Each applicant's total benefits also cannot exceed the property taxes paid on the home.
